column2: Basic Electronics for IoT and Microcontrollers

Fundamentals that apply to any microcontroller project, from a weather station to a robot: why modules read random numbers without a shared GND, how long a battery lasts, how to switch a relay from a 3.3 V pin, and how to check a circuit with a multimeter.
How to use this page

This page covers the electronics you actually use when building microcontroller and IoT projects: ESP32, ESP8266, Arduino, Raspberry Pi Pico, plus their sensors, relays, motors and batteries. It is not complete theory, but enough to understand why a circuit works, why it does not, and how to check it.
Read in order. Chapters 1 and 2 are the foundation for all the other chapters. Chapter 2 (shared GND) is the most common cause of "weird" circuits.
Answer first, then open the answer. Recalling it yourself before seeing the answer makes a concept stick better than rereading.
Do the exercises. The checkboxes are saved in this browser, and the status label on the main page changes with them.

A digital multimeter, one microcontroller board (ESP32 or Arduino), a breadboard, jumper wires, an LED, resistors (220 Ω, 1 kΩ, 10 kΩ), a button, and a battery (AA or 18650). A beginner ESP32 or Arduino kit usually has all of it. Every exercise uses low voltage. Never try anything on 220 V household power.
Voltage, current, resistance and power
These four quantities are behind every number in a module's datasheet.
Voltage (volt, V) is the difference in electrical "push" between two points. A single point on its own has no voltage. "A 3.3 V pin" means the pin is 3.3 V higher than GND.
Swipe the picture sideways to see everything.
Water flows because of a difference in height. Electricity flows because of a voltage difference between two points.

Current (ampere, A) is how much electric charge flows through a wire each second. 1 mA = 0.001 A. Current flows only when there is a closed path: out of the source, through the load, and back to the source.
Current is how much passes one point each second, not how fast a single drop of water moves.
Resistance (ohm, Ω) is how strongly something resists current. 1 kΩ = 1,000 Ω.
Same pressure, narrower pipe: less gets through.

The limits of the water analogy: use it only for visualizing. Electricity does not "run out" along the way: the current leaving the + terminal equals the current returning to the − terminal. A wire is not "empty" and then filled either; the electrons are already throughout the wire and move together as soon as there is voltage.
Ohm's law and power

Example: a red LED and a 220 Ω resistor on 6 V. The LED "uses" about 2 V, so the resistor carries 6 − 2 = 4 V. The current is I = 4 / 220 = 0.018 A = 18 mA, and the resistor heats with 4 × 0.018 = 0.07 W. Without a resistor, nothing limits the current and the LED or pin is damaged.
Try it yourself: Ohm's law in motion
Slide the voltage and resistance. Watch the current change, and the resistor turns red when the heat is large.
Voltage is measured across the two ends of the resistor. The current is the same at every point of a closed circuit.
Ohm's law calculator
Fill two boxes, leave one empty, then press Calculate. Resistance can be written 1k or 2.2k.

A multimeter on two Li-ion cells in series shows 7.8 V. That is the voltage between the red probe (+ terminal) and the black probe (− terminal), about 3.9 V per cell: the battery is reasonably charged. A full Li-ion cell is 4.2 V.
Check your understanding
Answer in your head first, then open the answer.
The multimeter shows 3.3 V with the red probe on the 3V3 pin. Between which points is that number actually measured?
Between the red probe (3V3 pin) and the black probe (usually GND). Voltage is always between two points; move the black probe and the number can change.
A 1 kΩ resistor is placed straight across 5 V. What are the current and the power?
A board draws 150 mA from 5 V. What is its power?
Measuring voltage and resistance
Closed circuits and shared GND
The most important chapter on this page. Most "weird" circuits turn out to have lost their return path.

Current travels around a loop: out of the + terminal, through the load, and back to the − terminal. If the path breaks at even one point (loose wire, cracked solder joint, switch OFF, blown fuse), current stops along the whole path. Switches and fuses work this way.
What GND is

GND (ground) is the point agreed to be 0 V. All other voltages are measured from there. In a microcontroller project, GND is the shared − terminal. It is not the earth and not the earth wire of household wiring, only a name for the reference point.
Voltages are like heights: the numbers only mean something if everything is measured from the same floor.
Signals need a return path too

When a microcontroller sends a signal to a module, that signal is a 3.3 V or 5 V voltage relative to the microcontroller's GND. The module reads it relative to its own GND. If those two GNDs are not connected, the module does not know "3.3 V relative to what". The signal has no return path, and the voltage the module reads floats: it changes on its own, affected by anything nearby, including your hand.
Left: the microcontroller from USB and the module from its own adapter, with no shared GND wire. Right: one GND wire closes the signal's return path.

Any two devices that send signals to each other must have a shared GND, even if their power comes from different sources. Only the GND is joined. The + terminals of different sources (USB 5 V, 5 V adapter, battery) must not be joined: two sources with slightly different voltages fight each other.

A servo is powered from a separate converter, the microcontroller from USB, and there is no wire between the two GNDs. The symptoms: one servo is still, one vibrates, and touching metal on the power line makes the servo move. The human body always picks up a little voltage from household wiring nearby, and a floating point is easily affected by it. One GND wire fixes everything. The same pattern shows up in motor drivers that will not run, relay modules that click by themselves, and sensors that read random numbers.
Two microcontroller boards send data to each other over UART (TX, RX). Each has its own adapter. What must be connected besides TX and RX?
The GND of both boards. Without a shared GND, the UART data is read garbled or not at all.
Can the 5 V from USB be connected to the 5 V from an adapter to make it "stronger"?
No. Two sources with slightly different voltages push current into each other, and current can flow back into the laptop's USB port. Only the GND is joined.
Why does a switch OFF turn off the whole circuit when it breaks only one wire?
Because current needs a closed path. A single break stops the current along the whole path.
Checking connections with the beep test
Series and parallel
Two ways to arrange components, and why every module on the same rail shares current from one source.

Series: connected one after another, the + terminal of one to the − terminal of the next. Voltages add, the current is the same everywhere. Two Li-ion cells in series: 3.7 + 3.7 = 7.4 V (nominal), 8.4 V when full. Four AA batteries in series: 4 × 1.5 = 6 V.

Parallel: all + joined as one, all − joined as one. The voltage is the same, the currents add. All modules on a 3.3 V or 5 V rail are in parallel: each gets the same voltage, and the source must be able to supply the sum of all their currents.
Series raises voltage, parallel splits current among several loads at the same voltage.
10 kΩ in parallel with 10 kΩ = 5 kΩ (always smaller than the smallest)

Three I2C modules are on the same bus, and each carries a 4.7 kΩ pull-up resistor. Those three resistors become parallel: about 1.6 kΩ in total. It usually still works, but the more modules, the smaller the total and the more current the pin has to draw. Another example: several LEDs in parallel sharing one resistor. The LED with the lowest Vf takes the most current and fails quickly. Give each LED its own resistor.
A 5 mA sensor, a 20 mA OLED display and an ESP32 averaging 80 mA are on the same 3.3 V rail. How much current comes from the regulator?
105 mA. Parallel: the currents add.
One of four AA batteries in series is installed backwards. Roughly what is the total voltage?
About 3 V, not 6 V: one reversed battery subtracts instead of adds (1.5 + 1.5 + 1.5 − 1.5).
What is the total of two 2 kΩ resistors in parallel?
1 kΩ. Two equal resistors in parallel = half the value.
Power sources and regulators
Where the 3.3 V and 5 V in your project come from, and why regulators can get hot.

Almost every microcontroller project needs more than one voltage: 3.3 V for the chip, 5 V for some modules, and sometimes 6-12 V for motors or LED strips. Those voltages are made from one source with a regulator.
Laptop USB or charger
a laptop port is usually 0.5-0.9 A; a thin or long cable lowers the voltage at high current
check the maximum current marked on it; the plug polarity can differ
AA alkaline battery
1.5 V each (dropping to about 1.0 V)
not rechargeable
NiMH battery
1.2 V each
rechargeable with a NiMH charger
Li-ion 18650 / LiPo
needs a dedicated charging module (for example TP4056) and protection
lasts longer, flatter voltage
only for small currents, for example an RTC or a sensor that is asleep almost all the time
Linear regulators and switching converters

When to use it

AMS1117, the regulator on ESP32 boards

A buck converter for the same example only throws away about 10-15% of its power as heat. A linear regulator also needs a minimum difference (dropout): the AMS1117 needs about 1.1-1.3 V above its output, so an AMS1117-3.3 needs an input of about 4.5 V or more.
Adjust the converter trimpot until the output voltage is correct before connecting a board or module. A new converter from the factory can output a voltage almost as high as its input.
The 5V, VIN and 3V3 pins on the board
VIN or 5V goes into the board's regulator. On ESP32 boards it is usually given 5 V. Check your board's documentation before applying another voltage.
3V3 is the output of the board's regulator. It can be used for small sensors, but the small regulator on the board is quickly overwhelmed if loaded with a motor or many modules.
Do not power from USB and from the 5V pin at the same time, unless your board clearly has an isolating diode. Current can flow back into the USB port.

The ESP32 board restarts by itself just as WiFi starts to connect, and the Serial Monitor prints Brownout detector was triggered. When transmitting, the ESP32 draws a brief current spike (its datasheet says up to about 240 mA). A thin or long USB cable, a weak port, or other modules on the same rail make the voltage dip for a moment until the chip resets. The fix: a better USB cable, a stronger source, a 100-470 µF capacitor near the power pins, and big loads on a separate source (with shared GND).
You apply 12 V to a module that uses an AMS1117-3.3 and draws 200 mA. How much heat is in the regulator?
(12 − 3.3) × 0.2 = 1.74 W. For a small regulator without a heatsink that is too hot. Step down to 5 V with a buck first.
A 3.7 V Li-ion battery will be used for a module that needs 5 V. Which converter?
A boost (step-up), for example the MT3608. Or choose a module that can work directly at 3.3 V.
Why should a motor and an ESP32 preferably not be supplied from the same regulator?
Motor current spikes lower the voltage briefly. If the ESP32 is on that line too, it can brown out and reset.
Measuring the power source
Power consumption and battery life
The calculation that separates IoT devices that last months from those that die within a week.

A battery-powered IoT device is seldom on all the time. It usually wakes briefly (reads a sensor, sends data over WiFi), then sleeps. What decides battery life is the average current, not the current while active.

Example: active at 120 mA for 5 seconds, then asleep for 10 minutes. If the sleep really is 0.01 mA (10 µA), the average is about 1 mA, and a 2000 mAh battery lasts about two months. If the board still draws 5 mA while asleep, the average is about 6 mA, and the same battery lasts only about ten days. That tiny sleep current turns out to decide everything.
Battery life calculator
For a device that wakes briefly (measures, sends over WiFi), then sleeps. Starting values: an ESP32 development board that still draws 5 mA while asleep.
The invisible current eaters
The power LED on a board that is always lit: several mA.
A linear regulator such as the AMS1117 draws several mA for itself (quiescent current), even when the load is asleep. For batteries, choose a regulator with a quiescent current of a few µA.
The USB-serial chip on a development board (CP2102, CH340) that stays powered.
